newsitem.title: UK: U.S. stocks in London banking on Dow rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks in London banking on Dow rise.

text.p: U.S. stocks in London did not trade on Monday but strategists were betting that Wall Street would continue its record run as investors returned to work from the long Independence Day holiday.
Automotive supplier Lear Corp, Boeing Co and the tobacco companies were expected to grab some interest, traders said, but price indications were not available.

The Dow industrial average soared 100 points on Thursday to 7895.81, after surging with the bond market on a surprise uptick in the U.S. unemployment rate to 5.0 percent in June. Economists predicted the rate to hold at May's 4.8 percent reading.
This week's most significant data, June's Producer Price Index (PPI) on Friday, is expected by U.S. economists to bolster the prevailing low-inflation scenario.
June PPI is expected to be unchanged, compared with a 0.3 percent decline in May.

"Given that the U.S. had a quite favourable employment report for June and given that the Fed decided to leave interest rates on hold, that is going to give some support for European markets generally," said Gareth Evans, equities strategist at Nikko Europe.

Lear could attract attention, after the senior portfolio manager of Citibank Global Asset Manager, Barbara Marcin, touted the stock in financial weekly Barron's. The stock closed down 1/8 at 42-7/8 on Thursday.
A European Union threat on Friday to block the proposed merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas Corp led to some interest in the U.S. aircraft manufacturer.
An EU source said its competition experts agreed that the merger should not go through if the companies do not make changes to meet the EU's anti-trust concerns.
Investors were closely watching tobacco shares in the aftermath of a settlement between the state of Mississippi and tobacco companies.
Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore on Thursday announced the $3.6 billion settlement and called on Congress and the White House to approve a $368.5 billion national accord.
